l: 먹기 전에 손을 씻으라는 말이에요.
먹는 동안 뛰라는 말이에요.
식사 후에 자라는 말이에요.

2.name: An idea worth sharing
2.focus: Follow the order and explain a simple reason.
words: a word that gives a reason
used to suggest a good action
a word used to ask for a reason
s: We should take some water.
Maybe it will rain later.
2.story: Hana asks why they need water for their walk. Min says they may feel thirsty because it is warm. Hana agrees they should take bottles. Maybe it will rain later, but they still need water to drink.
r: Is rain certain in the story?
l: 물을 좀 가져가는 게 좋겠다는 말이에요.
물을 모두 버리자는 말이에요.
걷지 말자는 말이에요.

2.name: Looking back and ahead
2.focus: Follow the order and explain a simple reason.
words: something you do that is not right
s: This feels hard at first.
I can try it again.
2.story: Catching feels hard for Min at first. He makes a mistake and looks away from the ball. Hana says to watch it. He tries again. Catching feels easier after practice, although he still misses sometimes.
l: 처음에는 어렵게 느껴진다는 말이에요.
처음부터 완벽하다는 말이에요.
다시는 안 하겠다는 말이에요.

6.name: Ready for class
6.focus: Compare ideas and support an answer with evidence from the text.
words: decide which task needs doing first
something that must be included or done
starting useful work without being told
being ready to explain and take responsibility for your actions
s: We should prioritise the tasks needed for tomorrow's display.
Taking initiative also means checking what our group needs.
6.story: A group must prepare a display by Friday. The only requirement is that every claim has a source. Aroha wants to decorate the border first, while Min wants to check the facts. They prioritise checking because an attractive display could still contain mistakes. Hana takes initiative by making a list of missing sources. Each person signs beside the facts they checked. This gives the group accountability: they can explain who checked what. They finish the border afterwards, using the time that remains.
r: Why do they check facts before decorating?
Every claim must have a source
They have already finished the display
Names beside the facts each person checked
l: They will do the most urgent display tasks first.
They will leave every task until Friday.
They will decorate without checking any facts.

6.name: Making friends
6.focus: Compare ideas and support an answer with evidence from the text.
words: understanding how another person may feel
making sure people can take part
talk to reach a plan both sides can accept
shared by both people or groups
s: We can negotiate a plan that includes both groups.
Empathy helps us notice needs that differ from ours.
6.story: Two groups want the same playground space. One needs a quiet area to practise a play; the other wants a running game. At first, each group calls its own activity more important. Hana asks them to describe what they need rather than who should win. This shows empathy for both groups. They negotiate different times and agree to leave a clear path. Their mutual plan supports inclusion because children can join either activity. A week later, they review the plan instead of assuming it suits everyone forever.
r: How does Hana change the discussion?
She asks about each group's needs
Why review the plan after a week?
People may discover needs the plan has missed
Only the first group can judge it
l: They will discuss a plan that both groups can accept.
One group will secretly take the whole space.
Both groups must choose exactly the same activity.

6.name: Lunchbox choices
6.focus: Compare ideas and support an answer with evidence from the text.
words: what food provides to help bodies grow and work
not too much or too little
something used in place of another thing
s: Check dietary needs before choosing food for our celebration.
We can substitute another ingredient without excluding our classmates.
6.story: The class plans a shared meal and discusses nutrition. A poster recommends variety rather than one perfect food. Students privately tell the teacher about dietary needs. The group decides to offer moderate portions, with more available if wanted. One recipe contains an ingredient a classmate cannot eat, so they find a substitute and check its label too. They do not ask the classmate to explain personal details publicly. The final menu includes several choices. Its success will depend on whether people can eat safely and feel included, not whether every plate looks identical.
r: It may also contain an unsuitable ingredient
What is the main purpose of several choices?
To include people with different needs
To make everyone eat the same meal
l: They will consider what classmates can eat before choosing food.
They will publish everyone's private health details.
They will choose food by colour alone.

6.name: A change in weather
6.focus: Compare ideas and support an answer with evidence from the text.
words: something done to reduce a possible danger
how much water vapour is in the air
how likely something is to happen
s: A forecast gives probability rather than a promise of rain.
Taking a precaution can help even when plans stay unchanged.
6.story: Two weather reports describe tomorrow's walk. One says rain is possible; another warns of severe wind on exposed hills. A parent notes that humidity alone does not tell them exactly when rain will fall. The class compares the reports' times and locations before choosing a sheltered route. Carrying coats is a precaution, not proof that rain is certain. They also agree to check an updated report before leaving. If the wind warning continues, they will change the plan. The children learn to separate the probability of an event from the possible harm it could cause.
r: The reports may describe different conditions
Preparation can be useful even when rain is uncertain
Humidity gives the exact time of rain
l: A forecast describes how likely rain is, not a guarantee.
A forecast makes the weather happen.
A forecast can never help with planning.

6.name: Finding your way
6.focus: Compare ideas and support an answer with evidence from the text.
words: find your way through a place
a different route around a blocked place
knowing where you are and which way to go
easy for people with different needs to use
s: We need an accessible route that everyone can use safely.
Use the map to navigate around the closed path.
6.story: A school group needs to navigate from the library to a park. The shortest path has steps, and one student uses a wheelchair. A map shows a longer accessible route, but part of it is closed. The group asks about a detour and checks that it has no steps. They use a visible clock tower for orientation. Although this takes more planning, everyone can travel together. The group decides that a useful route is not always the shortest one. They add the closure date to their notes so another group knows when to check again.
r: It has steps that exclude a group member
It is shown on a map
The route information may change later
l: They need a route that includes everyone's access needs.
They want only the fastest walkers to arrive.
They will choose the route with the most steps.

6.name: At the shops
6.focus: Compare ideas and support an answer with evidence from the text.
words: an amount taken off a price
how well something is made or works
money needed to pay for something
s: A large discount does not always mean better value.
Compare quality and total expense before making your choice.
6.story: The class acts as a group of consumers choosing lunch containers. One advert offers a large discount, but the sale container has a loose lid. Another costs more and has a lid that can be replaced. Students compare quality by testing both with the same amount of water. They also include delivery in the total expense. The cheaper price is attractive, but their notes show repeated leaks. They recommend the other container for carrying soup. Their advice might differ for someone who only carries dry food, so they explain the limits of their comparison.
r: Using the same amount of water
The recommendation depends on how the container is used
Leaking lids are required for dry food
l: A reduced price alone does not prove an item is good value.
Every discounted item is broken.
The largest discount always gives the best choice.

6.name: A fair playground
6.focus: Compare ideas and support an answer with evidence from the text.
words: treating people's needs and chances fairly
help people discuss a disagreement and find a way forward
what happens after a decision or action
s: A fair outcome may need more than equal turns.
We can mediate by listening before suggesting a solution.
6.story: A playground conflict begins when two teams disagree about extra practice time. One team missed its usual session because the court was closed. The other says fairness means equal time today. A teacher helps mediate by asking both teams to explain what happened. They agree on a short extra session for the team that missed out, followed by the normal timetable. The outcome is not identical time today, but both teams accept the reason. They record the arrangement so it cannot quietly become a permanent advantage for one team.
r: Why give one team extra time?
It missed a session because the court was closed
What is the passage's main idea?
Fairness may consider circumstances as well as equal amounts
Extra time should always be permanent
l: Fairness can require considering different circumstances.
Equal turns are never useful.
Only the winning team deserves practice.

6.name: Looking after things
6.focus: Compare ideas and support an answer with evidence from the text.
words: able to last through repeated use
make something as small as possible
the time something remains usable or alive
s: Careful repairs can extend the lifespan of our equipment.
Choose durable materials to minimise waste over many uses.
6.story: The class compares two covers for its outdoor books. A thin cover costs less but tears during a trial. A thicker one seems more durable. To preserve the books, students also bring them inside after each session. They realise that choosing a material is only part of the solution: care affects lifespan too. A volunteer repairs the torn cover so it can still be used indoors. This helps minimise waste without pretending every damaged item can be repaired. The class records future damage to check whether its first judgement remains useful.
r: What else affects lifespan besides material?
How the books are cared for
To check whether the judgement holds over time
l: Repairs and care may keep equipment useful for longer.
Only new equipment can ever work.
A repair makes equipment last forever.

6.name: Books we choose
6.focus: Compare ideas and support an answer with evidence from the text.
words: using something to stand for a larger idea
an idea suggested without being said directly
the feeling or attitude expressed by words
s: Which detail helps us interpret the character's quiet response?
The tone changes when the narrator notices the empty chair.
6.story: In a story, a child keeps an empty chair beside her at a concert. At first the narrator jokes about saving seats. Later, the child places a letter from her absent brother on the chair. The tone becomes gentle. Readers may interpret the chair as symbolism for someone being remembered. The implication is not that the chair can listen, but that the brother matters to her. Another reader might suggest a different meaning, but it should fit the letter and the change in tone. An interpretation needs clues, not just an interesting guess.
r: Which detail supports the idea of remembering someone?
The brother's letter on the chair
l: They need a detail that supports an explanation of the response.
They can choose any meaning without reading.
They only need to count the story's words.

6.name: Our school garden
6.focus: Compare ideas and support an answer with evidence from the text.
words: a planned test to find something out
an idea that can be tested
something that may affect a result
s: Our hypothesis needs a test with only one changed factor.
Record all the data, including results we did not expect.
6.story: Students design an experiment about seed growth. Their hypothesis is that more light helps seedlings grow taller. They use the same seed type, soil and water, changing only the hours of light. After a week, one seedling in the darker place is taller than expected. Rather than remove this result, they record it with the other data. They decide to test more seedlings before reaching a strong conclusion. Light may be a factor, but a small experiment cannot show that it explains every difference. Unexpected results help them ask better questions.
r: Why keep soil and water the same?
To make the light comparison clearer
To guarantee their hypothesis is right
What should they do with the unexpected result?
Claim the whole test proves nothing
l: A useful test changes one factor while keeping others the same.
A useful test changes everything at once.
A hypothesis must be accepted before testing.

6.name: A trip to the beach
6.focus: Compare ideas and support an answer with evidence from the text.
words: living things and their surroundings working together
soil or rock being worn away
the variety of living things in a place
s: A small change can affect several parts of an ecosystem.
Protect vulnerable plants while checking signs of coastal erosion.
6.story: A class visits a beach to study its ecosystem. Their guide explains that plants help hold sand in place and give small animals shelter. A shortcut crosses these vulnerable plants. Some visitors prefer it because it is quick; others use the marked path. The class photographs the damaged area without walking on it. They suggest a sign explaining erosion and biodiversity rather than simply saying Keep Out. They cannot prove from one visit that footsteps caused all the damage, but they can explain why protecting the plants is a sensible action.
r: Why might an explanatory sign help?
It gives reasons for using the marked path
It proves all damage has one cause
Which claim is too strong for their evidence?
l: Changes can affect connected living things and their surroundings.
Every beach change affects only one plant.
A small change is always harmless.

6.name: Getting around
6.focus: Compare ideas and support an answer with evidence from the text.
words: travel regularly between home and school or work
the next service needed to continue a journey
how many people or things something can hold
s: Check the connection time before choosing our new route.
A disruption may affect passengers differently across the same journey.
6.story: Students compare ways to commute to a sports centre. A bus disruption means one route now arrives after their train connection leaves. Another bus arrives earlier but has limited capacity. They ask the organiser to confirm enough seats before choosing it. Walking is possible for some students, but not everyone can manage the distance. Their final plan includes a later train and an adult meeting them. It takes longer, yet it works for the whole group. The students explain why a quick route on paper may not be the best practical choice.
r: Why does the first route no longer work?
It has too many empty seats
What makes the final plan practical?
It works for all group members
It has the shortest printed time
l: They should check whether one service arrives before the next leaves.
They should choose a route by its colour.
They should assume every connection waits for them.

6.name: Feelings and needs
6.focus: Compare ideas and support an answer with evidence from the text.
words: being able to recover and keep trying after difficulty
manage something so it stays at a useful level
feeling and functioning well in body and mind
s: Different coping strategies may help us in different situations.
Taking a break can support wellbeing rather than show failure.
6.story: After a difficult rehearsal, Min wants to leave the group. Hana suggests taking a quiet break before deciding. Their teacher explains that resilience does not mean hiding every feeling. Min practises breathing slowly to help regulate his response, then tells the group which part was difficult. They try a smaller section together. This coping strategy helps today, but Min may need different support next time. The group values wellbeing as well as finishing the performance. They agree that asking a trusted adult for help is a useful action, not a failure.
r: What does Min do after his break?
Blame a person who was absent
Which idea does the text support?
l: Different situations may call for different ways of handling difficulty.
One strategy must work every time.
Asking for help always makes a problem worse.

6.name: Working together
6.focus: Compare ideas and support an answer with evidence from the text.
words: give different tasks to different people
working together towards a shared goal
expected to explain and look after your part
s: We can delegate tasks while remaining accountable to our group.
Consensus means we can accept a plan, not prefer everything.
6.story: A group creates a guide for new students. They delegate writing, drawing and checking, but meet regularly so the parts fit together. Collaboration means more than working separately at the same table. Two students prefer different cover designs. They reach consensus by choosing the clearer cover and keeping the other drawing inside. Neither gets every first choice, but both accept the plan. Each member remains accountable for checking their work. When a mistake appears, they correct it together instead of using the task list simply to blame someone.
r: Use one cover and include the other drawing inside
They meet so their separate parts fit together
They never look at each other's work
l: They can share tasks and still take responsibility for their own parts.
Sharing tasks removes all responsibility.
Only the person drawing must check the work.

6.name: Making something tasty
6.focus: Compare ideas and support an answer with evidence from the text.
words: how much of one thing there is compared with another
how something feels when touched or eaten
a series of steps to do something
change part of something to improve or suit it
s: Keep the ratio unchanged when making a larger batch.
Modify one step so we can explain its effect.
6.story: The class makes a cold fruit mixture with adult support. The recipe uses two cups of yoghurt for each cup of fruit. When doubling the amount, students keep that ratio. One group adds extra fruit and notices a different texture. They write down how they modified the process rather than calling the result simply wrong. Next time, they will change only one amount so the comparison is clearer. They also check ingredients for dietary needs. Their notes should help another group repeat the method and decide which texture suits its own purpose.
r: How much yoghurt goes with two cups of fruit in the original ratio?
So others can explain and repeat the result
So every texture must be identical
l: Use the same relationship between amounts in a bigger batch.
Use the same total amount for every batch.
Add ingredients without measuring any of them.

6.name: Celebrating together
6.focus: Compare ideas and support an answer with evidence from the text.
words: why something matters in a situation
the features and connections that help describe who someone is
how people or ideas are shown
the effect someone or something has
s: Ask people how they want their community represented here.
An object's significance can differ between families and individuals.
6.story: Students prepare a display about celebrations in their community. One student brings a photograph and explains its significance to her family. Another celebrates the same event differently. The class realises that one example cannot represent everyone's identity. They ask contributors to check the captions and choose what may be shared. This gives families influence over their representation. The display includes both similarities and differences without ranking them. Visitors are invited to ask respectful questions rather than assume that a photograph explains a whole culture. Some families choose not to contribute, and that choice is respected too.
r: To help ensure their experiences are represented accurately
To make all families seem identical
To decide which culture is best
What does the second student's account show?
People may celebrate the same event differently
The first student must be wrong
l: They should ask how people wish their community to be shown.
They should decide everyone's identity from one photograph.
They should publish private stories without asking.

6.name: The world online
6.focus: Compare ideas and support an answer with evidence from the text.
words: how much a source deserves to be trusted
favouring one side in a way that may be unfair
s: Verify the claim using a source that explains its evidence.
A confident voice alone does not establish a source's credibility.
6.story: A video claims that a new drink makes homework easy. Its creator speaks confidently but also sells the drink. Min notices this possible bias. He looks for evidence and finds only comments from buyers. Hana checks a source that describes how learning was measured and notes its limits. They do not label every enthusiastic review deliberate misinformation, but they cannot verify the video's claim. The class discusses credibility by asking who made the message, why, and what supports it. They decide not to share the claim as a proven fact.
r: Why might the creator favour the drink?
What is the most justified conclusion?
The claim has not been verified by the evidence shown
l: Check the claim against a source that shows supporting evidence.
Trust the claim because it sounds exciting.
Count likes instead of checking the evidence.

6.name: Noticing the natural world
6.focus: Compare ideas and support an answer with evidence from the text.
words: members of one species living in an area
living things relying on one another
where things are found across an area
s: Compare the distribution of organisms across both survey areas.
Interdependence means a change may affect more than one species.
6.story: Students survey two parts of a reserve with a guide. One shaded area has many small organisms under fallen leaves. A sunny area has fewer of the same kind. They describe this distribution without claiming that shade alone explains it. Moisture and food may also matter. The guide explains interdependence: a population can be affected by changes to the plants or animals it relies on. Students leave the organisms where they found them. They plan another survey after rain, using the same search time in each area to make their comparison more useful.
r: Why avoid saying shade is the only cause?
Moisture and food may also affect the pattern
How will the next comparison be made more useful?
Use the same search time in each area
Search one area for much longer
Move all organisms into the sun
l: They will compare where living things are found in two areas.
They will count only the largest animals everywhere.
They will remove living things before observing them.

6.name: Changing our waste
6.focus: Compare ideas and support an answer with evidence from the text.
words: able to be replaced naturally over time
the effect an activity has on the environment
how well resources are used without waste
s: Reducing consumption can matter as much as choosing new materials.
Compare the whole process before judging its environmental footprint.
6.story: The class compares reusable lunch containers with single-use wrapping. A reusable container needs resources to make and water to wash, so its footprint is not zero. However, repeated use may reduce consumption of wrapping. Students count uses and discuss washing efficiency rather than assuming a green label proves everything. They learn that renewable resources can still be wasted if used faster than they recover. Their proposal is to care for containers already owned before buying new ones. They describe what they measured and what they could not measure, making their conclusion useful but limited.
r: Why is a reusable container's footprint not zero?
Making and washing it use resources
Which proposal follows from the comparison?
Stop recording how often things are used
l: Using fewer resources can be important alongside changing materials.
Buying more always reduces waste.
A new material has no environmental effect.

6.name: Moving and practising
6.focus: Compare ideas and support an answer with evidence from the text.
words: the ability to keep going during activity
getting strength or health back after effort
how well someone does an activity
s: Recovery time is part of practice, not wasted time.
Compare your performance with your own earlier efforts first.
6.story: Min wants to improve his running endurance, while Hana practises throwing coordination. Their teacher helps them choose different goals. They record their own performance over several sessions rather than compare unlike activities. After a tiring day, Min runs more slowly. The teacher explains that recovery and rest matter too. One slower result does not erase his earlier progress. They look for a pattern across the records and adjust practice gradually. Both students learn that useful evidence includes how they felt and the conditions, not only a final number on a chart.
r: Why not compare Min's and Hana's numbers directly?
What does one slower run show?
l: Time to regain strength is a useful part of practising.
Every break prevents improvement.
Practice only counts when someone becomes exhausted.

6.name: Solving a mystery
6.focus: Compare ideas and support an answer with evidence from the text.
words: show or say something that does not fit another claim
an idea reached by using clues logically
seeming possible based on what is known
s: A plausible explanation still needs evidence before we accept it.
Which clue might contradict our first assumption about the footprints?
6.story: A muddy footprint appears beside a missing class ball. Min's first assumption is that the last child outside took it. Hana points out that several children wore similar shoes. Then the caretaker reports moving the ball indoors before the rain. This detail may contradict the idea that the wet footprint marks the ball's removal. The group makes a new deduction: the footprint and missing ball may be unrelated. That explanation is plausible, but they check the indoor cupboard before deciding. Finding the ball there supports the new account without identifying who made the print.
r: Which detail challenges the first assumption?
The ball was moved before the rain
What remains unknown at the end?
l: An explanation that seems possible should still be checked.
A plausible explanation is automatically proven.
The first guess must always be correct.

6.name: Telling our stories
6.focus: Compare ideas and support an answer with evidence from the text.
words: a part of a story showing an earlier event
a clue suggesting what may happen later
the feeling created by a place or text
how parts of a text are arranged
s: The flashback explains why the character avoids the old bridge.
Look for foreshadowing before deciding the ending came without warning.
6.story: A story opens with a child refusing to cross an old bridge. A flashback shows that a loose board frightened her last year. Back in the present, a new warning sign creates an uneasy atmosphere. The sign also provides foreshadowing: later, the bridge closes for repairs. The structure lets readers understand both the child's feelings and the practical danger. If the earlier scene were removed, her refusal might seem unexplained. The class compares the two versions and uses details from each to discuss how the order of events changes a reader's understanding.
r: Why the child avoids the bridge
How much a new bridge costs
Which detail hints at the later closure?
l: An earlier scene helps explain the character's present choice.
The flashback shows an event that has not happened yet.
The child refuses because every bridge is closed.

6.name: An idea worth sharing
6.focus: Compare ideas and support an answer with evidence from the text.
words: a reason offered against a claim
an idea someone says is true
a response showing why an argument may not work
using reasons to connect evidence and a conclusion
s: A strong rebuttal responds to the reason, not the person.
Explain how your evidence supports the claim you are making.
6.story: Students debate adding a quiet playground area. Their claim is that it would give children more choice. A counterargument says it might remove space for active games. Instead of calling opponents unkind, Hana offers a rebuttal: a small unused corner could be tested for two weeks. Her reasoning links the proposed location to the concern about space. The class agrees to count use and ask both groups for feedback. The trial might support the idea or show that it needs changing. A persuasive argument allows evidence to affect the final decision.
r: Which concern does Hana's rebuttal address?
The price of every playground toy
Why collect feedback from both groups?
To judge whether the trial meets different needs
l: Respond to the other argument rather than attack the speaker.
Insulting the speaker proves a claim.
A rebuttal must ignore the other reason.

6.name: Looking back and ahead
6.focus: Compare ideas and support an answer with evidence from the text.
words: useful in a different task or situation
judge your own work using clear checks
change to suit a new situation
taking responsibility for your work or choices
s: Use clear examples when you self-assess your learning this term.
A transferable strategy may need adapting for a new task.
6.story: At the end of term, Min reviews two pieces of work. He uses a checklist to self-assess, pointing to examples rather than saying everything is good. He notices that checking sources helped both a science poster and a reading task. This is a transferable strategy, although he must adapt it for different sources. Hana chooses a different goal based on her own evidence. Their teacher says ownership means helping decide the next step and seeking support when needed. Neither child has to pretend learning is finished; reflection helps them plan what to practise next.
r: It helps in more than one kind of task
It only works on science posters
Choosing a next step using evidence and support
Claiming there is nothing left to learn
Letting someone else choose every goal
l: Use specific evidence to judge your own learning.
Give yourself the highest mark without checking.
Compare only with the fastest classmate.
